#1209. Gianluigi Donnarumma was signed to be world's best shot-stopper, but at Manchester City, he's merely fine

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Hard as it may be to believe or justify after events in Leipzig, there was a logic to Manchester City jettisoning their decade-long policy for goalkeeper recruitment last summer and signing Gianluigi Donnarumma. When your greatest defensive attribute is how your possession constricts your opponents from your third of the pitch then what you want from your No.1 is someone who can keep and progress the ball. Ederson is the dream. Even an aged Claudio Bravo is tolerable.

That all changed when Rodri's anterior cruciate ligament went in September 2024. Suddenly Manchester City were unable to shut down the opposition, to block off the counter and keep the other team to hitting and hoping. Having allowed somewhere around seven and a half shots in each of the previous four seasons, City allowed 9.34 in 2024-25, 9.71 in 2025-26. Now that Enzo Maresca has taken the helm and concluded that Elliot Anderson is enough of a midfield, we are at 10.56 in the Premier League. In the Champions League, where so many of City's opponents know best how to play on the front foot, it is 11 shots allowed per game (that average isn't as warped by playing PSG as you think).

If you're going to allow that much extra pressure on your goal, you want someone who can keep the ball out. In principle, Gianluigi Donnarumma is that guy, certainly if he is the player who carried Paris Saint-Germain through so many crucial moments and to their first Champions League title. But, of course, he isn't.

In Leipzig tonight, the outfield players managed to cover for their increasingly error-prone goalkeeper, Erling Haaland scoring a 13th goal in nine meetings with the Bundesliga side and earning a 3-2 win for City. Covering for Donnarumma was not something this team were able to do when he let Nicolas Jackson's shot through his gloves at Villa Park, nor when he got done by Desire Doue and Vitinha in PSG's heavy win at the Etihad.

Those errors betrayed a 6ft 5in frame with the manoeuvrability and burst of an 18-wheeler. Donnarumma might still be just 27 years old but his movement in recent months betrays every one of his 12 years as a first-team player, 553 games on the clock and a lot of rubber burned off those tyres.

You could potentially add Antonio Nusa's goal, Leipzig's second equaliser, into the category of shots Donnarumma might have got down to quicker. It's a 0.2 xG shooting position, one that the Norwegian hit fiercely enough that its post-shot value was 0.65. In other words, Donnarumma would have been doing very well if he saved it. This is, however, Manchester City's goalkeeper, one recruited for his shot-stopping above all else. You're entitled to expect him to do very well.

Especially when he was so cataclysmically clumsy for the first equaliser. Any goalkeeper's primary job is to protect his goal. In drifting three yards off his line when Riedle Baku was in a crossing position, Donnarumma was trying to take the easy way out. Again, a shot-stopper who is quicker to get down to the ball might have dealt with it. Certainly the Italian couldn't argue much that he had been unlucky; replays would suggest Baku saw the gap and hit it precisely.

Ridle Baku sneaks one in at the near post past Donnarumma 😤Stream the #UCL on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/tgP6KwASuh

Of course Donnarumma had had his moments earlier, a smart diving save denying Christoph Baumgartner's long-range strike. The same is true of this season and his City career as a whole. At his best, he has recovered that aura of his final months at PSG and across 56 games in the Premier League and Champions League, he has conceded six fewer goals than the post-shot xG value of the shots he has faced. In last season's Premier League he was one of the better pure shot-stoppers in the league; this time he is there or thereabouts.

As a whole, Donnarumma has been fine. It's just that he was not bought to be fine. If you're tolerating a goalkeeper who can't give you much at all in possession, it is because you want the best in the world at keeping the ball out. It seems like a long, long time since Donnarumma could lay claim to that moniker.

#1208. Trafford shows he has credentials to dislodge Pickford as England No 1

Has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford? It is a question worth asking after his brilliance secured his side a point against Sunderland.

Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.

After leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds. He is the most expensive British goalkeeper. More importantly, he is playing like it too.

This was a tough examination for Leeds, who were not at their best, against a typically robust and physically challenging Sunderland who are getting back to doing the things that made them so difficult to play against last season. Regis Le Bris’ side created the better chances but were repeatedly denied by Trafford.

With the windy weather playing havoc, ruining the game as a spectacle, as both sides struggled for control of the ball, the two moments of quality came from Trafford in the first half.

Goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

The first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

The second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

Robin Roefs is at it again with another important save for Sunderland 👏 https://t.co/SJ4qWmSHBo

Had the former Newcastle United player scored so late in the game, the home crowd’s frustration may have boiled over. The point means Le Bris’ side have still not won a league game since August and remain bottom of the table. This is proving to be a tougher second season in the top flight for Sunderland, but if they keep playing like this, they will not remain in the bottom three for much longer.

“It’s a positive [point],” said Le Bris. “The more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.”

“It’s a positive [point], the more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.

“It’s still a long journey, we know with this busy schedule playing in Europe, playing in the Carabao Cup, it’s a new challenge for us and we need to embrace it. I think we showed this afternoon that we are in this challenge, we want to embrace it and be ourselves and we probably deserved a bit more today.”

75.8% - The combined pass completion rate from today's @premierleague matches was just 75.8%. This is the lowest on a single day with 5+ matches played since 14th December 2019 (75.1%). 🌪️ Boelo. https://t.co/34WdKllPCH

"On another day we win" James Trafford assesses Leeds' 0-0 draw with Sunderland 🗣️ https://t.co/CZpftPCJSp

James Trafford speaks on his start to life at Leeds after another clean sheet 👏 https://t.co/E9wrzdheAD

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Sunderland man said: “I think the wind played a big part and credit to both defences and the attacks as well to be able to keep it to no goals in that swirling wind.

“I think it was a good effort from everybody so obviously we want three points from where we are in the table but keep putting up the performances like that and we’ll get some.

“As a defender it’s always nice to have a clean sheet and especially after the last few games where we haven’t had one.

“It’s always something we’re looking to do and Robin [Roefs] came up with some big saves, Omar [Alderete] coming on was really good as well and I hope my teammate’s [Nordi Mukiele] OK as well because I think that was kind of my fault. But we got the clean sheet for him so hopefully not too bad.”

When asked about Sunderland being bottom of the league, he replied: “I think always the table reflects fairly where teams deserve to be, and I think over the course of the course of the season if we keep putting in performances like that it will represent where we should be.

“But the table always reflects where people should be but we need to keep looking at ourselves, don’t look at other anyone else, it’s no-one else’s fault but us and we know that.”

That result means that Sunderland’s stay bottom of the Premier League and without a win in the competition since August 30, while Leeds earn their fifth draw in eight top-flight fixtures to move up to seventh on 11 points.

Full-time from the Stadium of Light as the points are shared between Sunderland and Leeds 🤝 https://t.co/ij9ioYEJH5

Ampadu’s cross finds its way to Okafor, who helps the ball into the danger zone towards Longstaff. The midfielder shoots from close range, but Sunderland throw in a couple of bodies to block it.

Talbi dreadfully overhits a corner straight out of play for a goal kick... that sums this game up.

Former Newcastle United midfielder Longstaff gallops forward and fires a low effort towards goal, but Roefs makes a great stop to tip the strike around the post for a corner. That was substitute’s first involvement after entering the action. Think it’s safe to say he wouldn’t be a popular scorer given his previous ties to Sunderland’s bitter rivals. There will be six minutes of added time.

Robin Roefs is at it again with another important save for Sunderland 👏 https://t.co/SJ4qWmSHBo

There’s a straight swap in Leeds’ midfield as Tanaka is withdrawn for Longstaff. This game appears destined to be 0-0. Can either side find a late winner?

Leeds make the next change as Nmecha replaces Calvert-Lewin up top. Trafford collides with Muharemovic as he comes out to claim a cross. He initially stays down and it looks like he has cramp, but he’s okay to continue and play resumes.

There are appeals for a penalty as Tutierov’s deflected cross hits Tanaka’s shoulder. It’s quickly checked and cleared by VAR.

It is rare you watch a game of football for more than an hour and cannot say with clarity who has been the better of the two sides. Sunderland have had their moments and Leeds’ James Trafford has been the busier of the two. Yet, Leeds have also had periods in the game when they have looked the more threatening and it has taken some valiant last ditch defending from the home side to deny them.

There’s a double change for Sunderland as Diarra and Talbi replace Angulo and Le Fee. Can either of these substitutes help the hosts claim a victory?

A double change from RLB 🔄 https://t.co/8E2MVJYLyM

On the turn, Tanaka swivels and shoots from just outside the penalty area. Roefs spills the fierce strike and Calvert-Lewin attempts to pounce on to the rebound. The goalkeeper gets another hand to the ball, preventing the striker from a tap-in. There are cries from the Leeds support up high in the away end for a penalty, but the situation is quickly checked and cleared by VAR.

Robin Roefs produced a quick double save to deny Tanaka and Calvert-Lewin from opening the scoring for Leeds 🧤 https://t.co/9otOjISuNh

Bogle bursts forward on the right flank and fires a powerful, teasing cross towards the back post. Okafor makes the run, but Sadiki is there to make a terrific interception and clear the danger.

Sunderland take advantage of the windy conditions as Trafford flaps at Xhaka’s looped corner. The ball drops to Angulo, whose low, driven half-volley is blocked by a sea of Leeds bodies.

Le Fee tries to slide an intricate pass through to Tutierov, but it’s cut out by Bijol, who reads the situation well.

Bogle catches Reinildo above his hip with a high boot. The referee gives the Leeds man a yellow card. Sunderland want something more. That was certainly a risky tackle from Bogle, who now must be careful.

Let's go, Timur 👊 https://t.co/JVxgPM7zAC

Attacking changes are here for both sides. Brobbey’s Sunderland return lasts for over an hour and he’s replaced by Tutierov. Meanwhile, for the visitors, Wilson and Aaronson depart for Stach and Okafor.

Bogle carelessly catches Angulo with a late tackle, gifting Sunderland a great chance to swing the ball into the box. Le Fee whips it in, but its flicked on and goes out for a goal kick.

This game is now being played at a much quicker tempo, with Justin bending an effort towards the far top corner. However, it drifts wide. Both sides look far more confident now and not like they’re playing for a draw.

At the other end, the ball breaks to Angulo, who stings Trafford’s palms with a fierce curling strike that forces the Leeds goalkeeper into conceding a corner. Excitement in this second half is starting to ramp up.

Leeds come forward again as Bogle tries to slide a low cross into Tanaka, but Le Fee tracks back to prevent the visitors from getting a shot off.

Wilson whips in a deep corner. Muharemovic wins the header at the back stick, but can’t get threatening contact on it and slowly directs it into Roefs’ grasp.

If I’m being kind to the players out there, playing in a strong wind at the Stadium of Light is notoriously tricky.

If you are watching on television, you might have noticed in the first half the litter being blown around in circles on the pitch. That will give you an idea of the conditions. The wind tends to swirl around inside this stadium rather than blowing in one direction. If I were any good at physics I would be able to tell you why. But I’m not. So I can’t.

Still, this match is yet to strike an attacking rhythm. Leeds have dominated the ball since the break, with Mukiele’s injury and subsequent departure slightly unsettling the hosts. Aaronson acrobatically knocks the ball across the six-yard box, but it’s hooked clear by Sunderland.

Mukiele won’t return to the action and heads down the tunnel. Alderete is on to replace his fellow defender. That is a blow for Sunderland to lose Mukiele this early in the second half.

We're forced into a change 🔄 https://t.co/ZJB0NOnawt

Mukiele is sat up and is still receiving treatment after being caught by O’Nein on his Adam’s apple. He walks off the pitch and it’s unclear if he’s able to continue. For now, Sunderland are down to 10 men.

The medical staff are waved on to the pitch as O’Nein accidentally catches Mukiele in the face with his outstretched arm.

We are back under way for the second half. Both sides are unchanged at the break.

Only two shots on target in that first half, with Brobbey forcing a couple of saves from Trafford. Hopefully we’re treated to some more exciting football after the break.

In a game lacking creativity and chances, nothing separates Sunderland and Leeds at the break. The best chance of the first half fell to Brobbey, but Trafford did well to smother the one-on-one opportunity.

There will be just one minute of added time to end this first half.

Nearly a disaster at the back for Sunderland as O’Nein lets a ball run thinking Roefs will come out to clear. However, the goalkeeper stays put. With Calvert-Lewin closing in, O’Nein has to make a last-ditch sliding challenge to direct the ball back to Roefs to stop the striker in his tracks.

Reinildo is booked as Bogle turns him, with the Sunderland defender dragging the Leeds man to the florr. He protests his innocence, and in fairness to Reinildo, he has a ripped shirt. He must be freezing.

Hume draws huge applause from the home fans as he crunches into a challenge on Gudmundsson. The Sunderland fans loved that sliding tackle.

Leeds are still waiting to record a shot on target. They’ve been pretty safe and unadventurous in forward areas so far.

A lot of huff and puff, honest endeavour and robust challenges in this game so far, but the two moments of quality have come from Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford. His first save to deny Brian Brobbey was excellent. He perfectly judged the trajectory of an awkward bouncing ball at full stretch, but I think the second is even better.

Trafford was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international but the way he stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb. He may have saved with his feet, but he cramped Brobbey for room and timed his moment to dive at his feet perfectly. That was elite level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Ampadu picks up the game’s first yellow card for bumping into Angulo on the edge of his own box. Sunderland now have a free kick in a promising position. Unfortunately for the hosts, Le Fee smacks it straight into the wall.

Sunderland’s pressure nearly pays off as Xhaka forces Wilson into a mistake. Brobbey is then too strong for Bijol and shrugs the defender off the ball. From a tight angle, the striker has a one-on-one opportunity against Trafford, but the Leeds goalkeeper does well to block Brobbey’s side-footed effort.

Sunderland fans are urging their side to press at every opportunity, cheering each time an intervention is successful. Still, we wait for the first notable chance.

Mukiele is down after being caught in the face by Calvert-Lewin as they both challenged for a high ball. There was no malice in the striker’s attempt to win possession and play swiftly continues following some quick treatment for Mukiele.

Mukiele was gearing up for a long throw, but the Sunderland defender held onto the ball for too long, with referee Attwell sounding his whistle to give possession back to Leeds.

Ampadu’s long throw-in casuses some momentary chaos in Sunderland’s six-yard box. However, the linesman’s flag is raised and Leeds’ chance disappears.

It’s been a scrappy opening to this game. Mukiele tries a very ambitious effort from long range, but he drags the shot well wide and it harmlessly trickles out of play.

O’Nein defends unconvincingly as he battles with Calvert-Lewin and attempts to deal with a long ball. The centre back just about handles the situation and prevents the striker from carving out a one-on-one opportunity.

#1207. Nobelitis — How winning a Nobel Prize can give you delusions of grandeur

After being chosen for one of the world's most prestigious awards, some Nobel laureates lose touch with reality and suddenly start spouting unscientific nonsense. They're afflicted by what some have called "Nobelitis."

Linus Pauling won not one, but two Nobel Prizes — the first, for chemistry, in 1954 for his research into the nature of the chemical bond, and the Peace Prize in 1962 for his work in the anti-nuclear weapons movement.

The American chemist not only won two Nobel Prizes, but won them on his own, a rare feat for any scientist. Such an honor often turns laureates into global superstars overnight, with millions hanging on their every word.

That instant fame can be dangerous, said Nils Hansson, a professor in the Department of History, Theory and Ethics of Medicine at Heinrich Heine University in Düsseldorf. Especially, he said, when these world-renowned experts "start spreading crazy, unproven scientific theories" — ideas that, when disseminated by Nobel laureates, risk being taken seriously.

That's what happened with Pauling. Beginning in the mid 1960s he began claiming that vitamin C was a universal remedy, a cure for everything from cancer to cardiovascular conditions and degenerative diseases like Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis or osteoarthritis.

Pauling developed an alternative treatment he called orthomolecular medicine, based on specific doses of vitamins and minerals for each patient. To this day, some 60 years later, evidence for his methods remains inconclusive.

Pauling's case is a classic example of "Nobelitis," or "Nobel disease" — not an official diagnosis, but an informal term used to describe how some laureates begin to suffer delusions of grandeur later in life. It was first coined by Paul Nurse, president of The Royal Society, the UK's national academy of sciences, and himself a winner of the Nobel Prize.

"Be skeptical of everything, including yourself and your own ideas," Nurse said in a 2019 interview with KU Leuven University in Belgium, when asked what made someone a good scientist. In cases of Nobelitis, that self-skepticism is the first to go.

That was also the case with virologist Luc Montagnier, who was jointly honored in 2008 for his discovery of the human immunodeficiency virus, HIV, with colleague Francoise Barre-Sinoussi in the early 1980s.

Montagnier would later go on to support homeopathic medicine, another alternative treatment of disease and claim that HIV transmission in Africa could be diminished through better hygiene and nutrition.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Montagnier said the SARS-CoV-2 virus had been created in a lab with parts of the HIV genetic code. "It's difficult for a practicing virologist to say that a Nobel laureate in virology is spreading nonsense," said German virologist Christian Drosten on NDR's Coronavirus Update podcast in May 2020. "But that is utter nonsense."

James Watson, who was never known for his modesty, also let fame go to his head. In 1962, he was awarded the Nobel Prize along with Maurice Wilkins and Francis Crick for their discovery of the structure of the DNA molecule. But in the early 2000s, Watson repeatedly spread racist theories that Black people were less intelligent than white people.

For medical historian Hansson, Watson is a prime example that the Nobel Prize is not automatically awarded to a person who should be considered as a role model.

"You may have made a fantastic discovery, but that doesn't make you a universal genius," he said.

But the great expectations of an admiring public may also contribute to the development of Nobelitis. Paul Nurse, who won the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine in 2001, soon found himself getting daily requests for interviews on all sorts of topics.

"As if suddenly I was acknowledgeable about all workings of the world and of human beings," he told DW.

Nurse had this advice for researchers: "Be careful quite what you say. Talk about things that you do know something about that would be fine. And if you don't know so much or you're not sure about something, be really clear that you're not sure."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hansson has also noticed that the media eagerly report whatever Nobel laureates say — even when prize winners stray far from their area of expertise.

Nobelitis sufferers are leaders in their fields and rightly honored for their work with the Nobel. But they're also regular individuals, not immune to megalomania and other behavioral problems — meaning that homeopathy, orthomolecular medicine and other pseudosciences don't automatically become credible just because they're backed by a Nobel Prize winner.

This article was originally written in German.

#1204. USMNT's Gold Cup path to look different as Concacaf unveils revamped group-stage format

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

For the United States men's national team to win their first Concacaf Gold Cup since 2021, they'll now need to contend with a new format in the 2027 edition. The tournament will run from June 17 through July 11, with major changes coming to the group stage. It will still include only 16 teams, but instead of those teams being split into four groups of four teams each, they'll now be split into only two eight-team groups. Fifteen of those teams will qualify via the Gold Cup preliminary round and join guest nation Saudi Arabia in the tournament.

That shift has the goal of making the group stage more exciting, as not only does it add an extra game due to each team playing four teams instead of three, but it also allows a chance for chaos, as four teams will go through to the knockouts from each group. While the new game is added, that won't change how the knockouts look, as those will proceed as normal.

"The Gold Cup is our region's premier men's national team competition, and we are really excited about what this new format will bring to the tournament's Group Stage," said Concacaf president and FIFA vice president Victor Montagliani. "Our fans want to see the best teams in our region compete against each other, and this format will create more opportunities for those matchups to happen earlier in the competition. At the same time, every match will matter, with teams facing a balanced mix of opponents and competing for a place in the knockout rounds. We believe this will make for a more competitive and exciting Gold Cup from the very first match through to the final."

How matchups are determined is where things get a little confusing, as they will organize the eight teams into ranking bands of two teams each, with a predetermined fixture matrix ensuring that each team plays a balanced schedule of opponents.

This is to prevent a situation where two strong Concacaf sides essentially ensure that others don't have a chance to advance, which could lead to more interesting fixtures in the knockout stages depending on how it goes.

🚨🏆 The rumors are confirmed! Gold Cup will have a whole new format in 2027. @FabrizioRomano breaks it down! pic.twitter.com/ydD1ZwbBvK

For the knockouts, nothing changes from how things used to look, as those four teams advancing from each group will then be placed into a single bracket, with the highest-finishing teams in each group facing off against the lower-finishing teams in the opposite group. There will then be no reseeding as the quarterfinals will determine the semifinal pairings in the road to the championship.

#1203. Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease

After a worker at a Russian plague research institute in Siberia died October 2, 2026, nearly 200 of her contacts were under medical observation. But authorities there denied pneumonic plague had caused the death.

UPDATE: Following initial reports raising concerns that a lab worker had died accidentally of pneumonic plague, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said it was now also "closely monitoring the situation."

However, in a statement published October 6, 2026, the ECDC said that "based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases and no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission that would cause further spread of the disease."

Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community.

Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information.

Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube.

She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia.

According to official Russian figures, authorities placed two hospitals and a children's clinic under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures."

All that is known for certain, at the time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious.

Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them.

The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague.

Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics.

Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood.

A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic plague go untreated and spread to the lungs.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is.

Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear the word "plague." It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people.

If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first.

Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms.

Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill.

Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says.

People close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague.

The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers.

They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

That is how far United have, once again, fallen. Fans in the Stretford End unfurled their “Standards” banner, bearing the faces of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and Bryan Robson.

It was first revealed in December 2021 in Carrick’s final match as interim following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s sacking. This should be his final game again, under different, more traumatic, circumstances.

If it is, he is going out having made a stand. He dropped Bruno Fernandes for his outspoken comments, aimed directly at Carrick and his tactics, following the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat away to Como on Wednesday.

At 2-0 down here it was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha when he substituted Youri Tielemans, who had been so terribly slow and ineffective, at half-time. Carrick did not bring on Fernandes. And he did not turn to the captain after, as he made four substitutions, including bringing on 19-year-old Shea Lacey. That said it all.

The television cameras catching Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, shaking his head in the stands as Carrick’s team gave away goals also told its own story. They have two wins from 12 in all competitions and none in eight. They have only beaten newly promoted Ipswich Town, in August, and Azerbaijan minnows Sabah this season. United were so careless it looked like they could not care less.

There was no guarantee, after Como, that Carrick would remain in charge after this game. So, losing and losing so embarrassingly – it was three, it should have been five – has to have obvious consequences. However cherished Carrick is. However much the fans excuse him. Yes, he has not been helped enough, but he has also not been good enough.

Finishing third and qualifying for the Champions League last season has proved to be the kind of bounce a new manager can achieve, after the pressure was relieved by the sacking of Ruben Amorim, rather than something more sustainable. There was always the fear that Carrick, despite his playing pedigree, might be out of his depth in this job. And so it is proving to be. Especially as he has been hung out to dry. Carrick certainly appeared resigned to his fate.

But what is he coaching? What is he trying to do with United? How does he want his team to play? Yes, there are limitations, but they are badly set up, tactically poor, and struggle to build attacks. The players are not responding, but it does not mean Carrick is blameless.

Bournemouth were not just collectively and individually better – and despite how good they are, that is some indictment of United – but better organised. They knew what they were doing, believed in it and relished it as they collected a fourth victory, and a fourth clean sheet in a row, after a slow start under Marco Rose, the new head coach. It was no shock.

The nature of the goals spoke volumes. For the first, a free-kick was needlessly conceded by Ayden Heaven, who endured a particularly difficult game, as he lunged in recklessly, forcing Evanilson to jump out of the way or risk injury.

Justin Kluivert whipped the ball in beyond the far post and it was met by Rayan, who volleyed in low and precise. The Brazilian was unmarked. Carrick protested – at what? – and the Bournemouth supporters sang “you’re getting sacked in the morning”.

The outstanding Rayan should have had a hat-trick but failed to take two chances in the second half, when he only had goalkeeper Senne Lammens to beat, after Bournemouth had already doubled their lead. It came as Leny Yoro slipped over and presented the ball straight to Adrien Truffert, who squared it for Marcus Tavernier to side-foot home. It was that ridiculously easy.

The third was the same, with Evanilson chasing down a ball forward by Tyler Adams. The striker should not have got there. But Harry Maguire, captain in Fernandes’s absence, gave up, pointing at Lammens to win it. Instead, the goalkeeper was beaten to the ball and Evanilson’s finish from an angle, arcing high into the net, was superb.

“You’re going down with the City,” goaded the Bournemouth fans and it is that end of the table United need to fret about. Which means, for Carrick, it has to be over. The Stretford End sang his name. But it was out of support for him as a player, his reputation, what he represented, not what is happening now as they once again vented their anger at the owners, director of football, Jason Wilcox, and even the plans for a new stadium.

It was the same as Carrick walked down the tunnel, thumping his chest as his name was sung. Then it turned. The vitriol, frustration and anger dripped down on the players, washing them away.

This felt like a new nadir. And the need for yet another new start away to Chelsea on Saturday.

Former Tottenham defender speaking to the BBC:

Manchester United’s players were just standing there today. I did not see in their body language that they are prepared to do everything for the manager, the club or the fans to change their situation.

It’s an easy thing to say they are lacking leaders but it’s true. They just don’t have big characters. It is not something technical but if you are in a tunnel and you saw the likes of [former Man Utd defenders] Nemanja Vidic or Rio Ferdinand their body language told the opposition that they were going to have a tough afternoon.

Carrick admits he does not know if he will remain in place.

The club have a week off now, with the next match a trip to Stamford Bridge against a tasty Chelsea side, albeit one who lost to Spurs last night.

He says: “It’s a tough situation. What is next? I don’t know. I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility. But we’ll have to wait and see.”

Carrick gives a non-answer over his choice to leave Fernandes on the bench.

He says: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference but those are the decisions we made today.”

Carrick then denies that his acknowledgement of the crowd was to say goodbye, adding: “It wasn’t a farewell from me. I’m mixed emotions, I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell.

“Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.”

Carrick also tells Sky: “It’s really difficult to have a day like this at this football club and feel the emotion and dynamics of what it was like today.

“Not for me personally but for Manchester United. It was really mixed. I feel responsibility with the position I’m in. I’ve been at the club a long time. It hurts a lot going through this.”

Carrick potentially acknowledges that his time is up, telling Sky: “It was a strange, mixed of emotions at the end of the game. It wasn’t a nice way to end the game.

“It was a tough day for the players. We went into the game having been rocked. You can feel that. They’re really hurting and disappointed in there. It’s not a nice feeling. You have to accept it, we’re in that situation.”

Today’s United captain Harry Maguire tells Sky Sports: “It wasn’t good enough. Disappointed to give a goal away so early - another set play - and conceding first in the Premier League it makes it difficult.

“A mistake for the second makes it hard for ourselves. We didn’t perform well enough as individuals or as a team and we didn’t deserve anything from the game.

“It’s not clicking at the moment. Results are not good enough and performances in the last week not good enough. Still early in the season.

“Got to find something, question yourself, look in the mirror - that’s the most important thing - think what you can do more and what more you can contribute to the team and if we do that we’ll get somewhere.”

United players have said this for some time now. Each season they look in the mirror, and each season the supporters get the same.

Telegraph columnist Jamie Carragher thinks Carrick has had enough after that.

His emotional exit after the match suggested as much, with the former Liverpool player telling Sky: “He wants to be put out of his misery tonight.”

The fact that a mid-table team can come to Old Trafford and leave with three points is no longer a surprise.

If anything, it’s unusual when competent teams struggle against United these days.

Quite how replacing a manager changes a decade of falling short solves things, who knows?

“If you looked at the difference to the Bournemouth team, you’d swap every single player for that Manchester United team. It was a poor showing.”

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

The move had looked likely with Carrick refusing to rule out stripping Fernandes of the captaincy when quizzed on the matter on Friday.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

#1199. Roy Keane shows softer family side in new holiday snaps

Roy Keane is renowned for being a tough character on and off the field â first as a player, then as a pundit â with crunching tackles and even tougher words down the camera.

But while he may be one of footballâs most feared hardmen, away from the game and with his family, heâs just like anyone else â a doting grandfather with a softer side.

Recently, the former Manchester United captain showed that side in full on Instagram, sharing a series of snaps from a family holiday to celebrate his 54th birthday.

Among the photos and videos were moments of Keane splashing around in the pool with his grandchildren, helping them build sandcastles on the beach, and smiling proudly as he held his youngest â and third â grandchild, born earlier this year.

The caption to his birthday post was as warm as the images themselves: "Happy Birthday to me. All the gifts I need."

For a man whose career was built on grit and steel, it was a rare public glimpse of the gentler moments that matter most.

Even the toughest captains, it turns out, have a soft centre.

#1198. An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging1,2,3,4, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an ‘add-on’ architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing various applications in synthetic biology and information storage.

#1191. As I sat in the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand, the raw emotion and magic of Old Trafford was all around me. It was a stark reminder that the fans and the place they flock to really are Man United's greatest gift, writes IAN HERBERT

Published: 07:00 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 06:22 EDT, 5 November 2026

The sound came rolling down in waves, crashing down around us as I sat in the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand, in the moments after Manchester United had conceded a most dreadful first goal. It was low and sonorous and quite extraordinary, really.

When a club go nine games without winning and fall behind again, you expect an air of sullen resignation – not that ‘UNITED’ which took hold and grew in a collective, magical act of defiance.

Much more would follow in a significant escalation of protest against the Glazers and their minority partner Sir Jim Ratcliffe. But in that moment – and once more when Roma’s second goal threatened to turn this into a catastrophe – it was just about the terraces and their team. A fanbase refusing to go gently into a night of quiet desperation.

Much has been made of the supposed need to let go of a history which has weighed heavy on this club since Sir Alex stepped away. In turn, United try to release it and then cleave to it again, blindly staggering around in their wilderness.

But on Tuesday night, in the stand bearing the great manager’s name, you looked around and were reminded of how the folk memory of Law, Best, Charlton, Cantona and Rooney is such a powerful weapon. It binds the fans back to what was once great. It is fuel.

What those fans brought into the stadium was not a naive and nostalgic sentimentality. They still demanded the best of the players. There is a clear acceptance among many that Bruno Fernandes is trying to repair things, but when he went down theatrically and protested about a challenge, he was told, ‘stop whinging’.

Michael Carrick celebrates Manchester United's victory over Roma on an incredible Old Trafford Champions League night

Matheus Cunha reacts after scoring United's third goal in their comeback win

This is a discerning, intelligent football public. ‘Standards’ is the word on that banner that’s been flying on the Stretford End.

But the collective view before kick-off was that if the players gave fully, then the fans were with them. ‘I just need to know they’re trying,’ said my friend Jocelyn, as we threaded our way through the crowds to the stadium.

Harry Maguire, who has lived this period of United struggle in the raw and was terribly exposed in a wretched first half, still wore that perpetual look of defiance on his face. When United were fatefully awarded the retaken penalty kick, some were saying that Maguire should be handed the ball. ‘At least he’ll put his foot through it.’

There was a frustration with the way that moments of promise broke down, as passes from Kobbie Mainoo and Carlos Baleba went astray. And with the time it takes Senne Lammens to decide how to distribute the ball, which slows United dreadfully. Yet a recognition of the fight shown by individuals who were patently playing for and engaging with the struggles of Carrick, while contending with a scorching scrutiny.

The shadow on the wall was the owners, of course. It was significant that the chants of derision for them struck up on the Stretford End each time United scored. As if to say that the green and gold campaign won’t fade with the slightest prospect of hope this time. There were tennis balls, balloons and a sense that something is building.

Even now, after 21 years, do the Glazers, hiding in their Florida redoubt, really know that they are playing with fire? This now feels as visceral as Liverpool fans’ hate for Tom Hicks and George Gillett Jnr, 20 years ago.

That club’s fans found ways of getting them out. They email-bombed every outfit that seemed ready to offer to help them, from Royal Bank of Scotland to US equity firm Blackstone. The audible boos when the tennis balls rained down after 20 minutes and five seconds – 20.05 represents the year the Glazers staged their leveraged buy-out – suggests protests affecting play are unwelcome for some and perhaps many. Yet the fury is unbridled. The centre may not hold this time.

The night, however, was about the power of this place to do extraordinary things. Even when Bryan Mbeumo crashed a golden chance to equalise against the post in the early stages of the comeback, you sensed something was afoot.

You’re so close to the pitch in the lower tiers of the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand that you feel you can almost reach out and touch the players. As the stadium gave, so they received. Fernandes marshalled. Youri Tielemans made a difference. Matheus Cunha seized the game by the throat.

Cunha and Shea Lacey race towards the jubilant crowd after United's third goal

And suddenly, like a river, that anthem was taking hold. ‘It’s Carrick you know. It’s hard to believe it’s not Scholes’ – over and over again

And suddenly, like a river, that anthem was taking hold. ‘It’s Carrick you know. It’s hard to believe it’s not Scholes’ – over and over again. At the end Diego Dalot was flat out on his back before us. Mason Mount, who’d been on the field barely five minutes, was in delirium and the post-match acknowledgement of fans by Carrick with his players felt like a victory lap. It meant that much.

The Carrick anthem was still being sung on the concourses as we flooded out under the clear night sky, and you knew for sure in that moment why no one wants the distinctly average names like Eddie Howe, Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann being touted for this job.

‘I don’t want us to start all over again,’ Jocelyn told me, still trying to compute what we’d just seen, after we'd joined the departing throng. ‘I want Carrick to do it. I want more nights like this.’

We learned in the aftermath that Carrick’s career-saving half-time speech had involved him telling his players how Old Trafford could do this. ‘I don't like to keep talking to the lads about what this place can do and the history and what's gone before too much, but it's there,’ he said. ‘This place does magical things. It's done it before and it'll do it over and over again.’

Yes, that really did encapsulate the essence of a night on which we discovered, once more, that the fans and the place they flock to really are Manchester United's greatest gift.

#1189. Nobel Prize in chemistry goes to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai

Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for their groundbreaking discoveries related to the origin of chirality and life's building blocks.

The Nobel Prize in chemistry on Wednesday was awarded to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis."

Kagan, who is 95 years old and was born in France, is affiliated with France’s Université Paris-Sud, and Soai, who is 76 years old and was born in Japan, is based at the Tokyo University of Science.

The scientists share the Nobel Prize for answering longstanding questions in chemistry about life's origins.

Specifically, the duo solved an age-old mystery that has long puzzled chemists: some molecules, like amino acids, exist as two variants that are mirror images of one another, but just one of the variants out of the two is found in living organisms.

The two answered questions about why life chooses one variant over another.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.

In chemistry, life's building blocks are what scientists call homochiral, after the Greek words for "same" and "hand."

The Nobel Committee said the chemistry prize recognizes discoveries that have enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

The duo's discoveries, the news release said, "have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals."

#1185. Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities1,2,3,4,5,6. Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male’s visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta’s strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster, where food odour can promote arousal7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta. Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant.

Social cues are essential for coordinating interactions between individuals, facilitating the emergence of group dynamics including mating, aggression and collective foraging8,9,10. Yet social interactions do not occur in isolation. Rather, they unfold in a broader environmental context that structures when, where and how social behaviours are expressed. Courtship and mating, for example, often take place at ecologically privileged locations—food sources1,2, prominent visual landmarks3,4 or suitable nesting sites5,6—where many individuals aggregate, either to increase their encounters with prospective sexual partners or to access key resources that promote reproductive success. In these settings, a central component of the environment is the social collective itself: the multisensory backdrop that emerges from the movement, sensory signals and interactions across all individuals in a group11,12,13,14. Social behaviours are therefore likely shaped by both the static properties of the physical environment and the dynamic features of the social landscape. Yet the neural mechanisms that integrate these distinct sensory streams to regulate social arousal states and structure interindividual interactions remain largely unknown.

The mating behaviours of Drosophila offer a powerful inroad to explore how animals adapt to complex ecological and social landscapes. Species in the Drosophila genus vary widely in their ecology and geographic distribution15,16,17,18,19,20, raising the possibility that mating strategies have evolved in concert with the diverse sensory environments in which reproduction occurs. Many species, including members of the Drosophila melanogaster subgroup, mate on their host plants, typically decaying ephemeral substrates where many individuals congregate17, creating a complex social backdrop for reproduction. Other species reproduce in more isolated social settings. Drosophila elegans, for example, establish individual territories and mate on their host flowers19, whereas species of the Hawaiian subgroup perform competitive lekking in the vegetation surrounding their hosts20. The evolution of Drosophila courtship behaviours may therefore have been shaped by the distinct sensory ecology of a species’ mating site and the structure and dynamics of the social groups that form there.

Reproduction and population density in Drosophila erecta, a close relative of D. melanogaster, are tightly linked to the seasonal availability of its host fruit—the screwpine Pandanus21—creating a narrow window of opportunity for individuals to meet and mate22. Such restricted access raises the possibility that D. erecta has evolved behavioural adaptations that couple reproduction to sensory cues emanating from its host, allowing environmental signals not associated with sexual communication to shape mating behaviour. Here we show that the olfactory volatiles emanating from a food patch exert both direct and indirect control over courtship in D. erecta. We find that food volatiles serve as a potent environmental trigger in this species, driving aggregation and serving as a stringent sensory gate to control a male’s sexual arousal. In parallel, environmental food odours shape the visual landscape in which courtship unfolds by encouraging males to approach and sample prospective mates, amplifying visual motion to transform the sensory backdrop of the social scene. D. erecta males are highly sensitive to this increase in visual motion, in contrast to D. melanogaster, pointing to the evolution of a multisensory feedback loop that coordinates male sexual arousal across members of the group, linking courtship to the broader social context. We show that species-specific differences in the sensitivity to environmental cues seem to arise from variation in how olfactory information impinges on conserved components of the courtship circuitry, indicating a potential neural substrate for the rapid tuning of sensory thresholds that govern sexual arousal. Together, these findings show how both ecological and social cues shape species-specific reproductive strategies. Moreover, our observations underscore that the social landscape forms an integral part of the environment—both reflecting the collective dynamics of the group and actively shaping the sensory experience of each individual in it.

To investigate how environmental factors shape the reproductive decisions of species with different ecological preferences, we compared the dynamics of groups of D. erecta and D. melanogaster (five males and five females) provided with a small patch of agar perfumed with food volatiles (diameter 21.5 mm) at the centre of a large arena (diameter 190 mm), a configuration intended to mimic the presence of a localized feeding site (Fig. 1a). Although D. erecta and D. melanogaster have distinct hosts and divergent olfactory preferences16,23, both feed on the yeast microbiota that metabolize decaying fruits and thus display attraction to volatiles arising from fermentation15,24. We therefore used apple cider vinegar (ACV), a broadly appetitive fermentation product, as a generic ‘host’ odour to compare how the chemical environment influences mating behaviours. Flies were fed and maintained as virgins in these assays to minimize their motivation to track towards the odour source for purely metabolic needs or in search of an oviposition site.

See Supplementary Table 1 for full statistics.

We found that in the context of the localized ACV patch, these two ecologically disparate species displayed distinct patterns of behaviour. D. melanogaster broadly explored the arena, giving rise to a dispersed spatial distribution where individuals interacted mostly in pairs and only intermittently in larger groups (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1a–e and Supplementary Video 1). By contrast, D. erecta individuals rapidly approached the central ACV patch and remained there for extended bouts (Fig. 1b,e and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b), forming dynamic clusters of three or more interacting flies (Extended Data Fig. 1c–e). D. erecta did not congregate on a patch composed of agar alone (Fig. 1b,e, Extended Data Fig. 1b,f,g and Supplementary Video 1), indicating that food volatiles act as a potent aggregation cue in this species. Consistent with the notion that aggregation serves a social function in D. erecta, more than 90% of their copulations occurred on the ACV patch, in comparison to the spatially dispersed mating observed in D. melanogaster (Fig. 1d,f and Extended Data Fig. 1h). Comparable differences in aggregation and mating behaviour were also apparent when D. erecta and D. melanogaster were presented with a food patch made from the ripe pulp of D. erecta’s native host Pandanus candelabrum (Extended Data Fig. 1i–l), aligned with evidence that ACV shares several key volatiles with the bouquet of fermenting Pandanus fruit25,26,27. Notably, D. erecta refrained from mating entirely in the absence of ACV or Pandanus (Fig. 1f), highlighting the importance of the food patch as a site of reproductive opportunities in this species.

The ACV patch could facilitate mating in D. erecta by simply aggregating individuals, creating a dense social landscape where interactions between males and females are enhanced by proximity. Alternatively, ACV may directly elevate the sexual arousal of males or females on their arrival to the patch. To differentiate between these possibilities, we assessed the courtship dynamics of groups of five males and five females confined to a smaller chamber (diameter 38 mm, 4% area of the large arena; Fig. 1g), allowing us to decouple the effect of spatial proximity from the influence of the chemosensory environment. D. melanogaster males courted vigorously in this arena, independent of the presence of ACV (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Video 2). By contrast, D. erecta males courted only when ACV was present but rarely in its absence, despite the high density of flies (Fig. 1h,i and Supplementary Video 2). Indeed, D. erecta remained dispersed on an agar-only patch (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 2a), with males rarely approaching or pursuing individuals of either sex (Fig. 1m and Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). In the presence of ACV, however, the spatial distribution of D. erecta individuals was transformed, displaying a pronounced peak at 3 mm (Fig. 1k)—the interfly distance characteristic of courtship pursuit—along with a broad tail, reflecting the dynamic interactions of males as they indiscriminately advanced towards any individual who came into their field of view (FOV) (Fig. 1m and Extended Data Fig. 2d). The rare instances of D. erecta courtship on agar were transient, in contrast to the persistent pursuit observed in the presence of ACV (Fig. 1l,m). ACV thus seems to influence mating behaviours in D. erecta not simply by aggregating males and females but by restructuring their social dynamics.

Different strains of D. melanogaster vary markedly in their sensitivity to courtship cues28. Nevertheless, several strains, including a Cameroonian isolate collected within the overlapping geographic range of D. erecta, courted vigorously even in the absence of ACV (Extended Data Fig. 2e), indicating that the lack of reliance on this environmental signal is a broadly shared trait in this species. Although the limited availability of D. erecta strains precluded a comparable analysis of intraspecific variation, these results indicate that the food volatiles of ACV in D. melanogaster and D. erecta cannot be readily explained by variation within species and instead point to species-level differences in the sensory control of courtship. We therefore extended our analyses to related Drosophila species with distinct host ecologies. Unlike D. erecta, its sister species Drosophila orena, which specializes on Syzygium waterberries18, the closely related generalist Drosophila yakuba16 and the more distantly related specialist Drosophila sechellia, which breeds on Morinda citrifolia17, all vigorously courted conspecifics in both the presence and absence of ACV (Fig. 1j). By contrast, ACV suppressed courtship in D. elegans, a specialist that reproduces on Ipomoea blossoms19, potentially reflecting the limited chemical overlap between ACV and the volatile bouquet of its floral host29. Thus, although the influence of the chemosensory environment on reproductive behaviours varies across species, D. erecta males appear to have evolved a unique dependence on food volatiles to promote their courtship.

How does the chemosensory environment transform the structure of the D. erecta social landscape? Because interactions between individuals were more frequent on ACV, we reasoned that food odours may heighten the salience of visual objects. To explore this possibility, we presented individual males with a stationary fly-sized target—a high-contrast hemispherical bead, 3 mm in diameter (Fig. 2a)—and assessed whether ACV altered their interactions with it. D. melanogaster males were largely indifferent to this visual target, independent of the presence of ACV, spending most of their time circling the perimeter of the arena. D. erecta males, by contrast, remained in close proximity to the bead, an effect that was enhanced by ACV (Fig. 2b,c, Extended Data Fig. 3a–d and Supplementary Video 3). Optogenetic activation of most olfactory sensory neurons using the Orco promoter (Fig. 2d), which replicates the attractive valence of ACV in D. melanogaster30, was sufficient to promote attraction to the bead in D. erecta males on agar, confirming that olfactory input underlies this shift in visual salience (Fig. 2e,f, Extended Data Fig. 3e,f and Supplementary Video 4). Visual approach was not enhanced by the same optogenetic manipulation in D. melanogaster males, underscoring that in D. erecta, olfactory input exerts a species-specific influence on how males interact with their visual surroundings.

Colour bar indicates relative density. c, Left, trajectories of males in b during the first minute after a fly comes within 3 mm of the bead. Schematics in d adapted from ref. 43, Springer Nature Limited.

Despite the strong attraction of D. erecta males to the bead on ACV, they frequently walked away before returning to it, generating a distinctive radial pattern as males alternated between approach and retreat (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Video 3), suggesting that the olfactory environment may also promote visual exploration. To examine this, we placed five D. erecta males in a large arena (diameter 190 mm) decorated with a lattice of 13 beads arranged in a regular square array (Fig. 2g; distance along edge 30 mm). In the presence of ACV, males spent most of their time near one of the targets but also frequently traversed between them (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i), often taking the shortest route (Fig. 2h–l and Supplementary Video 5). On agar, males restricted their exploration to a small fraction of the arena, remaining at their starting location or near the bead closest to it and rarely visiting any other visual targets (Fig. 2h–l, Extended Data Fig. 3h,i and Supplementary Video 5). Comparing the trajectories of solitary males showed that they display a similar shift in their behaviour in the presence of ACV (Extended Data Fig. 3j), indicating that visual sampling is driven by the chemical, not social, context. Without the bead lattice, males on ACV showed no spatial bias and remained broadly distributed across the arena (Extended Data Fig. 3h). By contrast, the visual exploration of D. melanogaster males was unaffected by the chemosensory environment (Extended Data Fig. 3k–o). Olfactory cues thus selectively promote exploration in D. erecta males.

Beads, although attractive visual targets to males, rarely evoked courtship displays such as the wing extensions associated with song production, indicating they are not perceived as potential mates (Extended Data Fig. 3p). Indeed, replacing a single bead in the array with a decapitated female shifted the search dynamics of males: on encountering the female, males often terminated their exploration and maintained her at close range (Fig. 2m,n and Extended Data Fig. 3q,r). Males occasionally resumed exploration of nearby beads after encountering the female but now often sang as they approached (Fig. 2o), indicating that the distinct cuticular pheromones carried by D. erecta females altered the males’ interpretation of visual targets, triggering a shift from exploration to courtship. Males on agar failed to locate the female in the bead lattice (Fig. 2p), suggesting that their limited exploration in the absence of food volatiles hinders their ability to detect or pursue prospective female mates. Thus, ACV promotes locomotion in D. erecta males to drive more frequent sampling of visual objects in their environment, supporting a form of ‘social foraging’ in which they search for reproductive opportunities rather than food resources.

In D. melanogaster, courtship is triggered by recognition of an appropriate conspecific female, a behavioural switch mediated by a network of male-specific P1 neurons that integrate multisensory signals—including direct excitatory input from pheromone pathways—to gate entry into a persistent arousal state31,32,33,34. D. erecta females, like their D. melanogaster counterparts, produce sex- and species-specific cuticular hydrocarbons35 that robustly excite the P1 neurons of conspecific males36, indicating that they similarly serve as chemical determinants of mate recognition. Food volatiles could therefore facilitate D. erecta courtship simply by encouraging males to approach females and sample their pheromonal cues. Yet even in the rare instances when D. erecta males initiated courtship on agar, their pursuit was fleeting (Fig. 1l,m), pointing to the possibility that food volatiles are required not only to promote encounters with females but also to sustain male sexual arousal in this species.

Consistent with this, although optogenetic activation of P1 neurons in D. melanogaster is sufficient to evoke persistent courtship37,38, in D. erecta it triggered only transient courtship bouts towards an immobilized female in the absence of ACV, with males rapidly resuming indifference after the optogenetic stimulus (Fig. 3a,b). By contrast, in the presence of ACV, P1 neuron activation drove sustained courtship in D. erecta males, suggesting that although P1 neurons promote entry into a state of sexual arousal, olfactory cues are required for its perpetuation. This olfactory dependence extended to pursuit of a moving visual target. In the absence of ACV, P1 neuron activation evoked only brief bouts of courtship towards a fly-sized 3-mm projected dot rotating on the floor of the assay chamber, whereas in the presence of ACV, males pursued and sang to the target spontaneously, even without P1 activation (Fig. 3c–f and Supplementary Videos 6 and 7).

To determine whether continuous olfactory input is required to sustain a male’s arousal, we leveraged the fact that tethered males will spontaneously court a fly-sized visual target projected onto a panorama, faithfully tracking its motion while singing to it38 (Fig. 4a). D. erecta males were largely indifferent to this visual target alone but initiated robust pursuit upon presentation of ACV (Fig. 4b,c,e,f, Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Video 8). Notably, courtship tracking was transient, with males rapidly terminating their pursuit at the offset of the odour stimulus, reinforcing that ACV is required for the perpetuation of arousal (Fig. 4e,f and Extended Data Fig. 4b–d). D. melanogaster males, by contrast, commenced courtship pursuit at the onset of the visual stimulus and persistently tracked it for the duration of the assay (Fig. 4c,e,f), consistent with evidence that visual cues are sufficient to arouse males of this species, even in the absence of further sensory feedback33,38 (Extended Data Fig. 5).
