Would have been a yellow for anyone else, I’d say, and the timing also made the referee reluctant.

This is a big day for Andoni Iraola and his emerging team and it feels like the stadium has its mojo back. It’s colourfully, lively and noisy and You’ll Never Walk Alone is being sung as loudly at any point since Liverpool were crowned champions in the spring of 2025. There is a feeling amongst home supporters that they fancy this today: that, in itself, shows progress because it wasn’t the case when Nottingham Forest and Fulham were the first Premier League visitors this season.

Any problems, he says, “let’s have a sensible chat” and he reminds them that they are responsible for their teams’ conduct as the strains of You’ll Never Walk Alone die down.

And now wreaths are laid in memory of the fallen followed by the Last Post.

Liverpool in Ron Yeatsian all red, Arsenal in that hideous faded yellow and blue. The yellow on Arsenal away kits should always be bright primrose. She didn’t wear a mustard ribbon did she, in the merry month of May?

Trey Nyoni is only the second ever teenager to make his first league start for Liverpool against the reigning English champions, after Raheem Sterling v Man City in August 2012. #LFC

The Arsenal players have long completed their warm-up and returned to the changing rooms. "He's brought a spirit that Liverpool really lacked last season" Jamie Carragher on the Liverpool fans taking to Ronald Araújo 🤝 https://t.co/dleLirsm2v

It’s not about me [being brave in picking Nyoni], it’s about Trey. In training he has shown he has the level. For us he’s very good without the ball. It’s a big challenge for him but [he is ready].

He is young but covers a lot of space. He is aggressive as well without the ball, calm in possession, good communicating with his team-mates which is good when you know how Arsenal play. You need a lot of change of marks [positions]. There have to be a lot of things done there in the middle and he has done that in other games.

The aggression we had [against Brighton, never resting] in their structures, we go again, recover, go vertical, attack the spaces in behind, win the chance battle, one v one situations. Don’t concede territory against teams like Brighton and Arsenal. We have to be as aggressive as we were in that match.

Teams like this don’t give you easy situations [to score]. We have to be good in one v one, shots from outside the box, finishes, set plays – we should be a team that is strong in set plays. You won’t get many chances against Arsenal and when you have one you’ve got to grab it.

Yes we had good results with Bournemouth against Arsenal but the strengths of my team in Liverpool are different so you have to approach it in a different way. There are things I can use [from Bournemouth] but not a lot.

Arsenal have lost three of their last four games against Bournemouth when Iraola was in charge.

We have been very close [to winning at Anfield in the last four seasons] but moments have decided those games. We have to be really precise in those moments for victory here and that has to be the case today.

Every manager has different solutions and a different approach and Andoni’s is very clear. We expect a different game to that one [last year when Arne Slot’s side won 1-0]. It is a team that is very vertical with a real capacity to create chaos from almost all situations. They’re very good in the high press with great individuals.

[On selection] We have had issues this week with ankles and other things and had to be smart how we manage the minutes today to have players for the minutes they are available for. The conditions and the context force you to make certain decisions [on Tzolis coming straight back in after a month out].

We can’t wait. This is the kind of opportunity, challenge, mission you want to come to Anfield for.

There will be a commemoration of the fallen and pledge to care for the living before the match.

Here is a question I did not think I would be asking at any stage this season: will Liverpool win the Premier League?

It would be premature to describe this Sunday’s Anfield fixture as a title duel. Arsenal are better equipped to defend their crown, while Liverpool are a work in progress.

Whatever the outcome this weekend, Arsenal will leave Merseyside as the overwhelming favourites to claim back-to-back titles. They have a six-point lead over Liverpool. Should that extend to nine, Andoni Iraola’s primary objective coming into this season will remain unchanged; qualifying for the Champions League will represent a promising start to his reign.

What makes this weekend more significant is the champions will find a different Anfield to that which ended last season in such a downbeat mood, and came into this one uncertain of what was in store.

The discussion about what is achievable for Liverpool in the coming months is evolving by the week, the team bubbling along slightly under the radar.

There are several reasons why there are those who believe Iraola’s side might push Arsenal closer than anticipated.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool, who start the game in fifth with 15 points, and Arsenal, six points in front of them in second place. Anfield, that glorious night in May 1989 excepted, has not been the happiest of hunting grounds for Arsenal and though their record there recently – three draws in the last four visits – has perked up, they have gone 13 seasons without a victory, so long ago, in fact, that Mikel Arteta was in the side that celebrated Lukas Podolski  and Santo Cazorla earning them a 2-0 win.

Having already lost within the perimeter of the historic county of Lancashire this week, when knocked out of the Carabao Cup on penalties by League Two Fleetwood Town, the champions will be keen to end that barren streak and go into the 4.30pm kick-off on the back of three successive league victories following their defeat by Brighton. Points today, one or three, will put them ahead of Manchester City at the top of the table while victory for Liverpool would allow them to overtake Chelsea and move one point behind Brighton, the team they beat last week with the kind of performance that inspired talk of a credible title campaign.

For the visitors Max Dowman is suspended after his red card at Highbury and Bukayo Saka and William Saliba are sidelined for at least another three weeks with injury. In his pre-match press conference Arteta noted concerns about Noni Madueke (ankle), Declan Rice (thigh). Riccardo Calafiori (unspecified) and Christos Tzolis who has returned to training but all are expected to be available. Andoni Iraola has ruled out Jeremie Frimpong as well as long-term casualties Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni and Conor Bradley but hopes to be able to include Dominik Szoboszlai and Victor Muñoz. Team news should come through at 3.15pm

#1073. Pressure mounts on under-fire Roger Le Bris as Sunderland lose again, Bournemouth's super-subs preserve their flawless start, Pierre Sage is handed a Crystal Palace lifeline after late equaliser, while Brighton win

By MILES STARFORTH and LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR and WILL PICKWORTH, SPORTS REPORTER and JAMES SHARPE

Published: 15:39 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 18:08 EDT, 5 November 2026

Sunderland's unbeaten start to their first European campaign in 53 years was brought to an abrupt end by Dinamo Zagreb to pile more pressure on Regis Le Bris ahead of Chelsea's visit to Wearside.

The Croatian side won 2-0 to heap more misery on Le Bris and his team at the Stadium of Light following a dismal start to the season in which his team has won just one Premier League fixture.

There were Bonfire Night fireworks across Wearside, and before the game at the Stadium of Light, but not enough on the pitch from Sunderland, who only came to life after the break.

Europa League football has been an antidote to domestic doom and gloom for Sunderland fans, with the club having made a bright start to its first European campaign in 53 years by winning two and drawing one of their first three group phase fixtures.

But it was Dinamo who would light up the first half with two moments of quality from Luke Stojkovic and Dion Beljo.

Le Bris had labelled the season as 'probably the most demanding challenge Sunderland has faced in its history' before the game, which followed a 3-1 defeat by newly-promoted Coventry City. The 3-1 loss left the Carabao Cup quarter-finalists rooted to the bottom of the Premier League with just five points from nine games, and Le Bris under scrutiny ahead of a challenging run of fixtures.

Roger Le Bris is under increasing pressure at Sunderland after seeing his side lose once again

Granit Xhaka cuts a forlorn figure as Sunderland's unbeaten Europa League start ends

Le Bris, mindful of Sunday's Premier League game against fourth-placed Chelsea, made six changes against the Croatian champions, leaving top scorer Brian Brobbey on the bench along with influential midfielder Enzo Le Fee.

Le Bris also labelled the club's domestic struggles this term as 'growing pains', and Sunderland are not the first promoted club to suffer second-season syndrome. The problem for them is that they also have to contend with a lot more games due to their success last season.

The Black Cats found Dinamo, who parted company with domestic double-winning manager Mario Kovacevic following a shock defeat by newly-promoted Rudes on Saturday, hard to break down in the first 15 minutes, and when Chris Rigg did get in behind after being found by captain Granit Xhaka, Jules Ahoka could not get enough power on his header.

Dinamo's Stojkovic, however, could not have hit his effort at the other end of the pitch any better. With Wilson Isidor waiting to come back on the pitch following treatment, the visitors, backed by 1,500 noisy fans, won a corner. Xhaka headed it away from goal, but only as far as Stojkovic, who chested the ball down and superbly volleyed it past Robin Roefs to put Dinamo ahead.

Thomas Meunier then clipped the woodwork with a cross aimed for the head of Isidor before things got even worse for the home side. Kevin Danso's weak clearance found Stojkovic, who clipped the ball to Beljo, who then dinked it over Roefs to put his team in control at the break.

Le Fee was one of four players sent on by Le Bris for the second half, and a goal from Isidor - he headed Xhaka's free-kick home - was ruled out for offside a minute after the restart.

Sunderland, at least, were playing with some much-needed urgency following a lacklustre first 45 minutes, and Danso hit the crossbar during a spell of pressure from Le Bris's side.

Sunderland fans vented their frustration, both at their team and referee Andrea Colombo, as the second half wore on.

Luka Stojkovic scored Dinamo Zagreb's opener in their 2-0 win with this sublime strike

But Sunderland, for all their second-half possession, rarely tested goalkeeper Dominik Kotarski, Dinamo saw the game out to condemn Sunderland to only their second defeat in European competition, the last having come against Sporting Lisbon in the 1973-74 season.

Le Bris must now quickly pick up his side ahead of the visit of Chelsea.

Progression in Europe is important for the club, and Sunderland should still avoid elimination when the Europa League's group phase ends, but nowhere near as important as preserving its Premier League status.

Forget the icing on the cake, the Cherries joint-top, second on goal difference, of the Europa League after their come-from-behind 3-1 win at Sparta Prague.

After winning just one of their opening eight matches in all competitions, Bournemouth have now won seven on the bounce thanks to second-half goals from Tyler Adams, Evanilson and Rayan. All three came on as second-half substitutes to underline the quality that Marco Rose has at his disposal.

'You can't get too comfortable. You have to continue to hold that standard,' reflected Adams post-match. 'That winning mentality becomes continuous, especially when you're playing every three days.'

Rose, who made eight changes to his XI, will be delighted with his side's fight but will also thank Sparta centre-back Tobias Guddal who inexplicably got himself sent off in the first half for two avoidable yellow cards.

Prior to Guddal's red card, Sparta were in the ascendancy and should have taken the lead when striker Jonatan Braut Brunes, Erling Haaland's cousin, inexplicably put wide a tap-in in the opening two minutes.

That was the biggest chance in the match until Bournemouth were awarded a penalty midway through the first half. Former Liverpool defender Ki-Jana Hoever, who is on loan from Wolves, was booked for a handball in the box. Lewis Cook's stutter run-up fooled Jakub Surovcik but saw his low effort hit the inside of the left-hand post before rolling out of play.

Evanilson was on the scoresheet as Bournemouth came from behind to win at Sparta Prague

Fellow substitute Tyler Adams (second left) started the visitors' 3-1 comeback with this finish

Rayan celebrates after adding a third for Bournemouth to complete their memorable victory

If Cook was unlucky, there was no element of luck to Sparta breaking the deadlock. Counter-attacking from a Cherries' corner, Surovcik threw the ball out to Ebrima Singhateh inside his own half. The impressive winger shrugged off Cook before beginning his brilliant run, which included slaloming in between Bournemouth players, and scoring. It was a goal befitting of the Champions League, let alone the Europa League.

Sparta's joy was short-lived as Guddal, who had already been booked for a foul on Ben Gannon-Doak, then inexplicably brought down Alvaro Rodriguez.

Rose turned to his bench at half-time and all of his changes worked as they pressed Sparta into mistakes. Adams was the beneficiary for their first goal as he scored with a low right-footed shot from outside the box 12 minutes after coming on.

With 10 minutes remaining Evanilson put the visitors ahead with a sublime curled effort into the far corner with no backlift.

'He's on fire right now, but you see him do it every day in training,' Adams purred about his team-mate. For him to do it in a game is no surprise. He has so much quality.

'Whenever he gets in and around the box, we're confident he's going to find the back of the net.'

Ebrima Singhateh scored the goal of the game to give Sparta the lead after a stunning solo run

Before Singhateh's stunner, Lewis Cook saw his penalty hit the inside of the post and go out

Evanilson then turned provider, via a neat one-two, to see Rayan score from distance.

The result means it's four out of four in the Europa League for the European debutants. With Celta Vigo away next after the international break, don't be surprised if it's five out of five.

As the fourth official signalled three minutes of added time, Pierre Sage may have been cursing his luck on the Selhurst Park touchline.

Although he has been hampered by the absences of Jean-Philippe Mateta, Ismaila Sarr and Dean Henderson at points this season, plus a transfer strategy that has left him shorn of experience and quality in key areas, the Frenchman was approaching a record of eight defeats in 13 league and European games.

Two seasons ago, Crystal Palace's hierarchy kept faith with Oliver Glasner when his side won one of their first 13 matches - a record that preceded the greatest 18 months in the club's history - but Sage was running out of time to prove he deserved a similar demonstration of trust.

Enter Daichi Kamada, Palace's best player here, as he finished calmly through the legs of Hoffenheim goalkeeper Oliver Baumann to rescue a valuable point for his side.

But this was a let-off for Sage on a night that had felt like it could precede the final days of his tenure, and he must now summon an improved display against Liverpool this weekend.

'Conceding early in the game was difficult because we had to push to come back,' Sage said post-match. 'But we scored at the end, and the players deserved it because they didn't give up.'

Daichi Kamara earned Crystal Palace a point in second-half stoppage-time against Hoffenheim

Hoffenheim took the lead in the 1-1 encounter when Alexander Prass (second right) scored

Palace's equaliser came when down to 10 men after Adam Wharton's (centre) earlier dismissal

There was nothing to sum up Palace's predicament quite like Alexander Prass' early opener. Having started well - with Kamada having a goal ruled out for offside - Quinten Timber saw a penalty appeal waved away before the out-of-form Adam Wharton was dispossessed. The German side broke forward at electric speed and Prass' effort squirmed through Henderson.

It was an all too familiar story as Palace's defence - weakened by Sage's decision to leave Axel Disasi out of his squad in what he later labelled 'an internal decision' - again looked ill-equipped for the challenge in hand.

'Offensively we did better than our two previous games, but we have to continue to improve defensively because we gave too much space to them,' Sage added.

'When we defend too much, we have no chance to exist in the game, and when we try to attack a little bit, we are quickly open. You don't exist in the game when you don't attack. For this team the best way to defend is to keep the ball with efficiency.'

The hosts were careless on the ball though, doing little to improve the subdued atmosphere at Selhurst Park, and although Yeremy Pino and Kamada spurned good chances, Hoffenheim appeared to have closed out the game.

Palace's late equaliser eases the pressure on under-fire boss Pierre Sage for now

Palace's frustration was demonstrated by four yellow cards in seven minutes, before Wharton received a second shortly after to compound their misery.

The home faithful threatened to turn restless and it looked like the night would end in disappointment, until Kamada's strike gave Sage a lifeline.

Trust Pascal Gross to seize the moment. For a little over an hour, Brighton toiled and laboured in pursuit of the goal that would ignite their European dreams.

The Seagulls have made light work of the Premier League, these vanquishers of Arsenal and Manchester City and now are starting to stretch their dominance across the continent.

Gnarly minnows Getafe love to make life deeply unpleasant for their opponents and Brighton, for all their energy and endeavour, looked destined to be unable to find the answers.

Yet there he was, this 35-year-old starting a remarkable 16th straight game of the season when it mattered. There was Gross, afforded too much space on the left, allowed to spot the run of Joao Costinha towards the back post.

Naturally, the German landed his raking cross right on Costinha's head. The wing-back nodded it across goal for Malick Yalcouye to send a header of his own into the top corner to win it and send Brighton, who are yet to concede in the competition, into the Conference League play-off places and their fans dreaming of European glory.

'The fans should dream and, hopefully at one point, maybe we fulfil their dream,' said Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler.

Malick Yalcouye (centre) scored the winner as Brighton won 1-0 at Getafe in the Europa Conference League

'We focus on work and we focus on the things we can control. We didn't play our best game. We had a few moments where we were lazy with the easy things. We didn't do the simple things on the highest level. But we kept a clean sheet, scored in the right moment and I think we deserve to win this game.'

Getafe, this modest club from the outskirts of Madrid, have long lived in the shadow of their monumental neighbours Real and Atletico but have also earned a famous reputation for a good old-fashioned giant killing.

They once beat Barcelona 4-0 here to overturn a three-goal deficit to reach the Copa del Rey final and then did them again in the league the following season. They went up the road to the Bernabeu in March and came away with three points.

Brighton, meanwhile, have made such a habit of turning over the bigger boys that, for the Seagulls, it's stopped becoming that extraordinary.

They mix so frequently among the giants these days that it's often easy to see the Seagulls as ones themselves. Getafe certainly would.

What was always going to be fascinating was the clash of styles. Brighton, with their relentless press and free-flowing football under Fabian Hurzeler, against a physical Getafe side that boasts the lowest possession and pass success rate in La Liga. There's a reason their players have already been shown six red cards

They certainly made it awkward for Brighton at times here. Bart Verbruggen was twice called upon to deny Getafe striker Ivan Azon in the first half – initially after some chaos inside the Brighton box and secondly after a desperately poor back pass from Olivier Boscagli on the stroke of the break.

Unlike in their Premier League exploits, Hurzeler's side struggled to find that bit of quality when it mattered.

Georginio Rutter, in his first start since August, fizzed a cross to the back post but it eluded Yasin Ayari, the hero of the Eithad, and then fired a shot of his own wide.

Heaven only knows how the ball didn't end up in the net when Jaouen Hadjam, Brighton's brightest spark, raced through on goal but couldn't beat the keeper or the post and Yalcouye's rebound couldn't find the gaping goalmouth.

Hadjam flicked the top of the crossbar with another effort in the second half before substitute Luka Vuskovic blazed another over.

Thankfully, as so often is the case, Gross was there to make it count.

#1071. FIFPRO report highlights growing pains in women's football

Expected global revenue of over $1 billion and new faces at the U17 World Cup show women's football is booming, but a recent report also highlights need for better structures globally.

At first glance, women's football is healthier than ever. A recent report by FIFPRO, football's global players' union, said worldwide revenue is expected to reach over $1bn (€894m) in 2027. The World Cup in Brazil, a first in South America, will be the last with 32 teams and is expected to be the most watched and biggest revenue-generating women's tournament ever.

The good news continues with the U17 Women's World Cup in Morocco, where the tournament is being held every year for five straight years. Germany, France, Spain, Brazil, the United States and defending champions North Korea are all at the 2026 edition of a competition whose reputation continues to grow.

"You can just see where the game is going, which is so exciting," US head coach Ciara Crinion told FIFA. "The level has just gone up. We have to continue to stay with that and compete as well. [The U-17 Women's World Cup] almost feels like that first stepping stone in a major tournament for young players, and now you see how serious it is taken."

Puerto Rico, Australia and Argentina are making their debuts. For Puerto Rico, qualification is historic, as no football team in the men's or women's game has ever reached a World Cup tournament before.

"We've embraced this idea of being Puerto Rico's first team to qualify for a World Cup," head coach Andres Mirabelli told FIFA. Alongside national development plans, player recruitment was aided by a diaspora of nearly four million in the United States, perhaps the strongest place for women's football in the world. According to FIFPRO, the regional football average salary in North America is $5,940 (€5,547) per month, which is far higher than any other continent.

But even for the handful of players who make it out of these youth tournaments to a professional career, creating a living out of the beautiful game remains a real challenge. The aforementioned FIFPRO report details that many professional female players across the world barely earn minimum wage, with some even falling below it.

The report, which sourced its data from player surveys across the world, found that only 66% of professional players are paid for 12 months a year. The global average salary is $2,600 (€2,300) a month, but the range varies drastically across the world. In Eastern Europe, for example, that average is $880 per month. In Africa, it is $432, but in North America it is just under $6,000.

"I think what you also find in the women's game is the gaps are not just between the top five leagues and the rest. There is a gap there, but even within leagues themselves [there is one]," FIFPRO head of research and strategy for women's football Frankie Brown told DW.

"In some of the other leagues you're dealing with teams that are operating professionally, so will be paying their players on a reasonable wage, and playing in the same league as them you'll have players that are on amateur contracts and not being paid at all."

With economic and job security an issue for many, the report reveals that psychological stress factors are now the second main reason many consider leaving football.

"This is one of the most concerning parts of the report," Alex Culvin, the director of women's football at FIFPRO, said in a statement.

"Of the 49% of women’s football players considering leaving the sport early, 46% cited their mental health as the reason. In interviews, players say the sport's growth brings new pressures — including extra workload and social media abuse — but that clubs do not have the necessary safeguards in place to support these changes. We want clubs and national associations to provide mandatory mental health support focused on wellbeing, which is independent of sporting performance objectives."

FIFPRO's report is asking FIFA to set a so-called floor for the women's game so that minimum standards in key areas such as contracts, pensions and health can be enforced. Perhaps inspiration can be taken from the labor deal the WNBA agreed in 2026. It was long-negotiated deal that ultimately sent a message to female athletes everywhere to push for better pay, conditions and a greater share of the revenue they help generate.

"It is positive that average salaries are increasing for some players and that more are earning a satisfactory wage, but it’s important to note that there is a huge disparity in pay across regions," said Culvin.

"There is also an imbalance in conditions, not only across the globe but also within regions; in Europe, for example, the difference in standards between the east and west is enormous. This is a gulf we need to work hard to narrow; the growth in the most advanced markets must not be completely isolated from the rest of the industry.

With high hopes for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil and recent moves to increase professional football domestically, Germany is aiming to become an example for structural improvement in women's football. Hosting the Euros in 2029 certainly gives them an incentive to improve standards.

While salaries are in the upper tier — in the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year — the process of structural development in the country is still in its infancy. A new German football association rule shows that even basic professional structures are still being established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.

"The facilities and the staff members," Nicole Anyomi told DW, were a factor in her making a recent move to London City Lionesses. "We have 30-plus staff members here whereas in Frankfurt we had like seven or eight. You can learn from each person and there is something new to learn every day. I think that's how you develop as a player faster."

Ultimately, the faster the game grows, the greater need to close the gaps.

"Despite playing on different continents, players are connected by their precarity," Culvin said. "The redistribution systems in women's football need to be more effective, touching more players and supporting a more sustainable ecosystem."

#1069. Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns

Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

“I have to take the responsibility,” he said. “We did not transfer the things we did in training. Hitting long balls all the time, that was not the plan. We were not brave enough to play short passes.

“As soon as the referee blew his whistle, the plan disappeared. We could feel the anger and the frustration, I felt it on the touchline. We are low on confidence and it shows.”

Newcastle looked listless, clueless and alarmingly devoid of belief in what they were being asked to do. They have the unmistakable whiff of a team in decline.

If they do not start playing a lot better, they will be worried about a relegation battle. It is four defeats in their last five games and the confidence in Jaissle to find solutions is fading. Rather than change what he is asking his team to do, he has doubled down on the formation and tactics.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight new signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

There was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

Everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

A rising shot from Merlin Röhl briefly had goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek worried. A free-kick into the Newcastle box caused panic. James Tarkowski won the first header, but Thierno Barry swung and missed with his left foot.

The groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

This is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

It was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

He did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. Tyrique George was played in far too easily from a free-kick but his shot should have been saved by Hornicek. It was straight at the Czech, but it went through him and it left Barry with a tap in. Newcastle appealed for both a foul on Fabian Schar and an offside but got neither.

Newcastle tried to gain some momentum and finally created a chance. Harvey Barnes curled a cross to the far post. It bounced awkwardly but Anthony Elanga somehow failed to bundle it across the line.

Joelinton’s shot from the edge of the box is struck powerfully and is blocked by Tarkowski, going behind for Newcastle’s first corner of the night. Hall’s delivery beyond the back post finds Burn but his header from just a few yards out goes wide. Burn should really be hitting the target from so close to the goal.

We are just a quarter of an hour into this one but you can already sense some frustration from the home fans. Everton, despite being away from home, have settled well into this game.

To sum up the frustration from the home supporters, Dedic plays a dreadful long free-kick into the box that has far too much on it and goes behind.

Under the lights at home, you would assume Matthias Jaissle would have wanted a fast start from his side but that has not happened for the hosts.

Barnes is afforded space to cut inside from the left and, from the corner of the penalty area, clips a dangerous ball towards the far post. There is slightly too much on it and the ball goes behind for a goal-kick, although for a moment Pickford appeared to be panicking. That is the second time Barnes has been given too much space to cut inside and if Everton keep allowing that, you would imagine that they will eventually be punished.

The two starting XIs are fairly similar to the ones that started on Thursday night but the obvious difference between the League Cup tie and tonight’s Premier League encounter is the change of ground. How big an impact can the Newcastle fans have on the outcome of this one?

Unsurprisingly, former Sunderland goalkeeper Pickford is roundly booed by the home crowd upon his first touch.

Ahead of Remembrance Sunday this coming weekend, with this being Newcastle’s final home league game before then, St James’ Park pauses to remember all those who have given their lives to protect this country. The Last Post is played after St James’ Park falls silent.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off from St James’ Park. Here is a reminder of how the sides line up this evening:

“I think everybody who has been in football and comes to St James’ Park knows what the atmosphere is like here. We have to try and quell it the best way we can. Newcastle have got some really good players. It is a Premier League game, we know a lot about them, they know a lot about us. I do not think there are too many big surprises tonight.”

“We picked up on what we can do better [against Everton], this is something we focused on in training, really committed in the last few days so hopefully we can deliver today.”

On Anthony Elanga returning to the starting line-up:

“It is important now after he was out for a long time with an injury. Now he is improving a lot physically and also getting the feeling to play with the lads again. Therefore he deserves to start today and hopefully he can put his potential on the pitch.”

On Will Osula starting after an injury scare:

“He is such a talented guy, young lad, he can cause any opposition problems so hopefully he can deliver that again with his strength.”

On what he is hoping for tonight to get the three points:

“Be clinical, ruthless in both boxes. Defend with everything you have and then be efficient and use every opportunity to score and then I think we will see a great result today.”

“That helps us for sure. The extra motivation and extra energy will be there from the stands and that is something that we can always count on here at home in our stadium.”

“Nothing more than what I am sure you have already heard so he is not in the team tonight.”

For Newcastle, a win tonight would take them up to seventh, just two points behind Chelsea in fourth. Despite the heavy away defeats and unconvincing performances, that would be an impressive start for a new manager. Matthias Jaissle has already felt the full force of the contrasting emotions on Tyneside in his three months in charge but big questions hang over his team. In particular, the “vertical football” style he brought from the Red Bull coaching school in Germany.

A defeat tonight, coming so soon after the 3-1 defeat in the Carabao Cup to Everton, will intensify the criticism of his approach.  It would also suggest Newcastle, despite all their positive talk over the summer, are nothing more than a mid-table team who will be looking over their shoulders rather than upwards this season.

A win for Everton will have the same uplift for David Moyes at Everton, also taking them up to seventh in the table. Newcastle and Everton meet for the second time in matter of days as the Premier League weekend concludes in the north east at St James’ Park. These teams encountered each other on Thursday night in the League Cup, where Everton won 3-1 at the Hill Dickinson to progress to the quarter-finals in that competition.

Newcastle, who won 2-0 at Crystal Palace in their last league outing, come into this game in 12th, with the chance to rise to seventh with a victory tonight. Their boss Matthias Jaissle has called on his players to use the defeat against Everton on Thursday as fuel for tonight.

“Now it is about taking that frustration into motivation for Monday and having that approach for the rematch,” Jaissle said. “We take it as a long-term journey, and our approach is to make progress, to see improvements. Now it is time to learn fast out of the mistakes that we just did. [There are] other phases where we can already see that we improved and this is something we can count on, we can build on, the good part. But football is also in the end about results so you need to avoid these simple mistakes.”

Everton, who have not won in the league since a 1-0 victory over Ipswich back in September, begin the night in 14th but, like Newcastle, could rise to seventh with a win. There are just two points that separate Bournemouth in seventh and Everton in 14th. Despite getting the better of Newcastle the other night, Everton manager David Moyes has warned that game will count for nothing tonight.

“It is a different ball game,” Moyes said. “Go to St James’ Park, on a Monday evening, they will get a crowd up there, you always know you are up against it. But we will go with confidence. We have played Newcastle a couple of times this year and done well, so we have to try and continue it. But Newcastle have got some really, really good players and players you have to concern yourself about.”

Jack Grealish was left out of Everton’s squad for that League Cup victory because of an unauthorised absence from training and the 31-year-old is not expected to be involved tonight.

These sides were involved in a dramatic fixture on this ground last season. Everton claimed a 3-2 victory, with Thierno Barry earning them all three points in the 83rd minute, moments after Jacob Murphy had equalised for Newcastle. Team news from St James’ Park to follow shortly.

#1065. Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief

As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that.

With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon.

That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne.

The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said.

Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined."

Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler.

But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war.

Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars.

"If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said.

In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel.

He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps.

Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets."

Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months.

According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel.

But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on.

Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky.

Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home.

The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports.

At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries.

Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan.

"There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions.

"An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski.

"Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added.

Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact.

According to calculations by the platform The World Data, the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels.

Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand.

"I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement.

Russia would normally export almost 10 times that volume if its refinery fleet was not being targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks, he added.

Canada also supplies diesel to the United States. Roughly 80% of all US diesel imports come from its northern neighbor.

Given Trump's verbal attacks on Canada and the ongoing trade dispute, analysts view the prospect of Canada supplying significantly more diesel to the US as highly unlikely.

This piece was originally published in German.

#1062. Liam Rosenior says Chelsea sacking had 'nothing to do with football' as he raises questions about 'tolerance' in England in first revelations about being axed just three months into the job

Published: 06:37 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 18:17 EDT, 5 November 2026

Liam Rosenior has claimed he was treated unfairly during his doomed 106 days in charge of Chelsea, and that the way it ended in disaster had ‘nothing to do with football’.

Rosenior was relieved of his duties after losing five consecutive games without scoring. The fifth defeat in that run – a 3-0 loss at Brighton in which Chelsea did not even muster a shot on target – saw the players accused of downing tools to get rid of their head coach. He lasted 106 days in total.

However, Rosenior, now manager of Paris FC, who are fourth in France’s Ligue 1, has claimed his Stamford Bridge sacking was 'nothing to do with football' in a cryptic comment about 'tolerance' in English football.

The 42-year-old Englishman took aim at ‘the media’ in particular as he said in an interview with So Foot: ‘It was the best experience of my life, and the hardest, too. It was fantastic, even though it only lasted four months. I don’t want to go into details now. I’ll talk about it one day, when the time is right. But in a country where tolerance is an important value, what happened there has nothing to do with football.’

Pressed to explain, Rosenior continued: ‘I know, I answered without answering it. Actually, the moment that worried me the most was at the beginning, when we went through that five-game winning streak.

Liam Rosenior was seen passing a note to Alejandro Garnacho with Chelsea 8-2 down on aggregate against PSG - and the reaction to it clearly still rankles with him

Then-Chelsea manager Rosenior was compared to The Office star David Brent online

‘Any club would have been happy with such a run, but not Chelsea. You get good results and you’re in the spotlight. Then, there was a kind of snowball effect in the media.

‘They made fun of those instructions I gave (Alejandro) Garnacho on a scrap of paper when we were down to 10 men against PSG (during the second leg in March as they lost 8-2 on aggregate).

'The clothes I wore became a joke, the way I spoke, too. I’m not a joke! You’re the first people I’m talking to about this, and probably the last for a long time, but one day, I’ll tell you what really happened.’

It is unclear whether by ‘the media’, Rosenior meant those reporters who covered the club or social media, where he was routinely mocked and referred to as ‘LinkedIn Liam’.

Those within the actual Chelsea pack who attended Rosenior’s press conferences believe he was treated kindly despite the Blues boss not helping himself at times.

For example, his decision to suddenly drop Robert Sanchez for Filip Jorgensen backfired, especially in their Champions League last-16 first-leg loss away at PSG. When Jorgensen was then injured, Sanchez returned to the starting line-up with his confidence having been dented.

Rosenior also created a stir when he argued with a member of Arsenal’s support staff for encroaching in Chelsea’s half during their warm-up before the second leg of their Carabao Cup semi-final. He accused his opponents of breaking the ‘etiquettes in football’ afterwards.

After his players huddled around the referee Paul Tierney in the centre circle before a Premier League loss to Newcastle, Rosenior defended their pre-match routine. He described it as being designed to ‘respect the ball’ – words which were also ridiculed on social media, even if that idea did originate from Willie Isa, Chelsea’s hire from rugby league.

The former Strasbourg manager is now enjoying life back in France as manager of Paris FC

Rosenior added in his interview that he was never accepted in the Premier League, saying: ‘In England, there’s this preconceived notion of what a Premier League coach should be, how he should behave. You have to conform to that standard. People who know me know that I’m someone who tries to be sincere and authentic.

‘But I don’t have control over how the media describes me or talks about me. What I’ve understood now, and this is important for all coaches worldwide, is that social media, or the media in general, can dictate public opinion about the quality of a player or a coach.

‘This isn’t new, of course, but the biggest lesson from my time at Chelsea is knowing that they are also capable of constructing the entire narrative around a club’s trajectory.’

#1059. Man Utd show fight on night of chaos to give Carrick a glimpse of hope

So maybe there is some fight left in the old dog yet?

At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.

Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford. A fifth defeat in six matches and the club’s longest winless run for 48 years beckoned. It was toxic on and off the pitch.

And then something changed. United, from being a dishevelled, disorganised mess, suddenly seemed to remember who they were supposed to be and what they were supposed to represent. Surrender gave way to fight. A team that had been feeling sorry for themselves discovered some pride. A crowd that had been baying for blood turned Old Trafford into a bear pit of a very different kind, and Roma simply did not know what had hit them.

This club have served up some famous comebacks over the decades, but it was hard to think of too many occasions when the mood and momentum had shifted this violently from one half to the next.

United fans were in open revolt in that first half, releasing green and gold balloons in protests before kick-off and then throwing tennis balls on to the pitch amid furious chanting against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. The players looked like they would rather have been anywhere else.

And yet by the 86th minute Matheus Cunha’s wild celebrations were encapsulating a wild night, the Brazilian ripping off his shirt after his dramatic winner before launching himself into a delirious crowd drunk on the euphoria of a victory that had seemed improbable in the extreme at the interval, when boos cascaded from the stands.

Whether this proves little more than a thrilling, heroic interlude in the endgame for Carrick, or the start of a genuine turnaround, is hard to know. And, let’s be clear, there was so much about the first-half performance to concern the hierarchy, who came under persistent, furious attack from fans at war with an ownership it reviles and wants gone.

But the second half stood firmly at odds with the shambolic display that had preceded it and suggested all may not be quite lost just yet.

Aston Villa visit Old Trafford on Sunday in the final game before the international break and, if Carrick can follow this with another win, then it will be intriguing to see where the Old Trafford board goes from there.

Carrick may at least have been encouraged by some of the things Bruno Fernandes said after the game, not least that he warranted being dropped against Bournemouth. And it was the captain who kick-started the fightback against Roma, albeit at the second attempt.

He had won the penalty after being fouled by Gianluca Mancini only to then contrive to miss it. But a retake was ordered for encroachment and, given a second bite at the cherry, Fernandes made no mistake.

When Carlos Baleba pulled up with a hamstring injury within seconds of the restart as he burst into the penalty area, Carrick must have wondered what else could go wrong.

But as United went hell for leather, the home supporters who had spent much of the first half attacking the owners and staging a number of colourful protest acts, suddenly found their voice in a very different way.

From being an atmosphere in which the players clearly felt cowed, Old Trafford was now rallying behind its men in red – and it helped to shake Roma in the process. They had been such good value for their lead, but now they were rocking, and United smelled blood.

There was wave after wave of attack as Roma desperately and often frantically tried to defend their goal, and it took a bad mistake from Leonardo Balerdi, who swung at thin air from Fernandes’s cross and missed the ball, to hand Cunha the chance to equalise.

Cunha was booked for taking off his shirt as he crowd-surfed bear-chested among the fans and was then sent off minutes later after a poor challenge. A fittingly chaotic end to a crazy night for the match-winner.

The difference to those opening 45 minutes was as stark as it gets. Indeed, the first half felt like a continuation from the fans of their blood-letting against Bournemouth.

When the clock hit 20.05 – a nod to the year 2005 when the Glazers bought the club – a pile of tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch from the Stretford End amid chants of “We Want Glazers Out”. They were quickly followed by cries of “Just like the Glazers, Jim Ratcliffe’s a c---” and “sell the club and f--- off home”.

Jason Wilcox, the club’s director of football, again copped for it. A banner read: “For the love, not the ‘likes’”. When the Champions League music played, hundreds of green and gold balloons – a reference to the club’s original colours and the 2010 protest movement – were released.

On the pitch, United were all over the place. Carrick had dropped Lisandro Martínez after his red card against Chelsea but his replacement Ayden Heaven was at fault for the first goal after getting sucked in and failing to check his shoulder. Had he done, he would have seen Matías Soulé unmarked and in acres of space with Diogo Dalot, United’s left-back, caught high up the pitch. Soulé made no mistake with his finish.

At that point, no one could have reckoned on the comeback that followed. Where it leads, who knows.

Speaking after the match, Michael Carrick was very positive about his side’s performance.

“It was a good night. I have to a lot of credit to the players for starters, showing that character and that quality when we needed it and to the supporters. This place does incredible, magical things,” said Carrick.

“I thought we grew into it the first half  after giving the goals too easily. We spoke at half time about how this place can change, it only takes one moment and it certainly did that and the boys made the most of every opportunity and were fantastic in the end.”

Asked about how he inspired the team at half-time he kept it simple: “Just not to get too disappointed about things. I thought we were coming into the game, getting around their box and it didn’t feel that way to the players because they were carrying too much frustration and disappointment and I knew we were doing some good things in the game against a really good team.

“Playing against man-to-man as much as they are, you probably get more failure than success and it’s still being positive and the boys responded so well to that.”

As for whether this will change United’s momentum now, he was cautious not to get carried away.

“Listen it’s one game. It depends on what happens next and we’ve got to capitalise on that but tonight the boys showed an awful lot,” he said.

“And I thought we came out the second half, unfortunately with Carlos having to go off and Youri coming on the pitch and I thought he was fantastic, he showed everything that he is as a personality, as a character and with his experience to step in the game like that, and the boys just went with the flow and you could feel how positive it was and it was nice to see this place like that again.”

Captain Bruno Fernandes also spoke after the match, acknowledging the difficulties the team has faced.

“It’s tough to say something at the moment to be honest. It’s been a tough period for us, we have not been able to play in the way we want, get the results we want. We’ve done some good bits, but not had the consistency to do it through a whole game to get results and it’s been tough.

“But today was important to get a win. We knew after that we still had the fans with us, we felt we could change it with a goal and something and fortunately we did it today.”

As for his penalty miss and re-take: “First one didn’t go the way I wanted, I did something wrong but I got a second chance and I cleared my head and my mind was only on to get the ball in back of the net.

“It’s been tough for the fans, we understand that. Having that belief from their side helps the team a lot and today was one of those days that Old Trafford came alive.”

After his first start as he returns from injury, Kobbie Mainoo was full of praise for the fans, saying he cherished the relationship the team had with them.

“It’s unlike anything else. We’d do anything for these fans on the pitch, all the love they give us throughout the season it’s only right we repay them and it’s a bit of fun just jumping into the stands with them.”

Speaking to Amazon after the match, Youri Tielemans said: “There has been a lot of pressure on him [Carrick] and that’s how we repay him, with a comeback like this, big character, big fight.”

“We just kept working, we kept believing. We were on the front foot in the second half, we tried to push them into their goal and we succeeded.”

As for whether or not the performance would be enough to keep Carrick in his role at United: “That’s a different question. The only thing we can do is stick behind him, fight for him and fight for the club.

“At the end of the day we are on the pitch and we need to show what we are capable of and tonight, especially in the second half, we showed what we can do and we turned up the gears.

“Let’s hope this is a good turnaround for us and let’s hope we can build on this.”

Manchester United fans are planning a series of in-stadium demonstrations at Old Trafford tonight in protest at the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s ownership.

Thousands of green and gold balloons – a nod to the club’s original colours as Newton Heath – are set to be released from the Stretford End when the Champions League music plays out ahead of kick-off.

There had been plans to bring a banner into the stadium bearing the words: “No new stadium, we want new owners” but that was blocked, apparently on the grounds of Uefa’s inability to sanction it in time.

The Glazers and Ratcliffe have come under growing attack this season with the club’s regular match going supporters at war with the owners.

A separate fans’ group has also been encouraging fans to join in anti Glazers and Ratcliffe chants in the 21st minute or, more specifically, after 20 minutes and 5 seconds: 20.05 is a nod to 2005, the year the Glazers completed their hostile takeover at Old Trafford.

#1058. Manchester City, the UAE and the UK's PM in a political tangle

Nearly 20 years after arriving in England, Manchester City's UAE owners could exit amid cheating charges. That would pose a challenge for a city — and prime minister — closely tied to Abu Dhabi.

Defiance was the word that stood out as Manchester City returned home for the first time since they were found guilty of 114 financial charges by the Premier League in a case that's made headlines around the world.

City showed a measure of it on the pitch, even as they lost 4-2 to holders, Qatari-owned Paris Saint-Germain, in the Champions League group stages on Wednesday.

Among the home fanbase at the Etihad Stadium, DW found universal support for City's Abu Dhabi owners — headed by Sheikh Mansour, who is also UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister.

"I'm all in with the ownership now," said local fan Matt. "If we end up back in League Two [fourth tier], so be it. We've got 15 years of memories we wouldn't have otherwise and to me it's just an accounting line on a spreadsheet really."

The stadium name itself is a reminder of the takeover that changed this club, and its part of Manchester, in 2008. The national airline of the UAE, Etihad's inflated sponsorship of City is among the key planks of the case against them, while many buildings and businesses around the stadium bear the brand. It's a stadium that's also seen plenty of success of late.

"We've seen things other fans will never see," added fellow City fan Josh. "I think people have got to consider how many people this club has given great memories to, how many people's lives have been changed by it, myself included....you've got to be grateful for that."

Though many in sky blue shared those sentiments, most outside the club now view the trophies won in the relevant period as tarnished. On top of that, critics point to City's reticence in providing evidence in their case, the long-documented human rights abuses in UAE and the often dismissive tone with which the owners have dealt with being found guilty of charges they have now appealed.

But those City fans appear to have one powerful ally in British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Though he has since sought to tone down his position on Mansour and co. somewhat, the former mayor of Greater Manchester said he "would be really concerned to lose them," after the verdict was announced in late September. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester," he added.

While Burnham has since denied being close to City's ownership, even as City were playing on Wednesday, The Guardian reported a club representative was invited on a government-backed trade delegation to India this week by Burnham's successor as Manchester mayor, Bev Craig.

Earlier the same day, Burnham was forced to confirm he had two additional dinners with the club chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium, having previously declared those only as matchday hospitality. It has become a serious domestic issue for the man who replaced Keir Starmer in July.

What is clear is that Burnham welcomed Abu Dhabi investment during his time in charge of the northwestern city. This came mainly in the form of residential and commercial buildings as well as libraries and sports centers, all popping up in previously run-down areas in and around the stadium.

Georgina Blakeley, a Professor at the University of Huddersfield who wrote a book called "The regeneration of east Manchester," told DW that UAE investment has transformed swathes of the city.

"One of the prime drivers for building this partnership with the Abu Dhabi United Group [a private equity arm of the state mostly concerned with the football club] was that at that point in time, 2014, there was no other private investor willing to invest at the scale that the council wanted. And to do so in a way that created a build-to-rent market," she said.

The UAE investment in Manchester, accelerated by the Manchester Life Partnership with the city's council signed in 2014, has been a key defense for the City owners and fans when faced with sportswashing allegations in the past. And while Blakeley believes councils in the UK are often forced to seek foreign investment, there has been some pushback on how east Manchester has changed.

"A lot of people would be critical of some of the developments in [the districts of] Ancoats and New Islington and say that it's gentrified the area and there are some tensions between newer populations coming in and living in the more expensive flats and those already there. I think there's some truth to it. But I also think there's some truth to the fact that people forget really, really quickly that if you go back to just the 1990s, Ancoats was a no-go area," she said.

While profit for both council and state have certainly been a driver of the partnership, Blakeley thinks that forging greater links to the community could be something City's owners see "as a beneficial side effect."

After 18 years in the club and city, the UAE are deeply embedded in this part of Manchester. With political ties between the UK and UAE now reportedly strained as a result of the charges, there are suggestions that City's owners will try to sell the club. They may also be forced to do so, with sanctions still to be decided pending City's appeal.

There is no such trouble at PSG, who look capable of winning a third straight Champions League powered by their own Gulf-State coffers.

What is clear is that state-owned football clubs can become successful fast in a free market, as the Premier League was when the UAE owners arrived. Deep pockets, strong contacts at the top tables of the sport and canny strategies to integrate with the local area can be a heady mix.

It's certainly one that's proved intoxicating to City's fans, who brush off secret second contracts, sham sponsorship and unreliable witnesses with a loyalty built on success, community and investment. Judging by the mood in Manchester on Wednesday, no sanctions are going to change that.

#1057. Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums

Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?

At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.

GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.

Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.

"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.

GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.

Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.

"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."

This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.

BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.

So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?

Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.

Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.

Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.

While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.

"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."

Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.

A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.

Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.

"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.

Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."

"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.

Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.

In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.

A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.

"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.

European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.

Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.

"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.

"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.

Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.

"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.

To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.

"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.

"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."

#1056. Brazil's elections matter for the planet. This is why

Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide. With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.

Few national elections carry as much environmental weight as Brazil's presidential race. And this one is being watched from far beyond the country's boundaries.

Home to the largest section of the Amazon rainforest, Brazil is guardian of a carbon sink of vital importance, making the country's conservation policies globally relevant.

Environmentalists have already voiced alarm at Flávio Bolsonaro — son of right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro — coming out 2% ahead of incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of elections.

"It's going to be a second coming of Bolsonaro, therefore a more radical Bolsonaro," said Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Climate Observatory, a network of Brazilian NGOs.

"At the risk of sounding alarmist, I would say Lula's re-election is the only thing standing between us and the end of the Amazon."

The Amazon rainforest stores huge amounts of the carbon dioxide (CO2) released into the atmosphere from the burning of fossil fuels. As a result, it helps regulate the Earth's climate.

For decades, the tropical forest has acted as one of nature's most powerful defenses against climate change. But it has also suffered from widespread deforestation.

During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, from 2019 until 2023, environmental agencies were weakened and enforcement efforts curtailed, meaning tropical forest was cleared at unprecedented rates.

"The environment agenda was disregarded and the level of control the government had on pollution overall, but specifically on deforestation, was reversed," said Claudio Forner, head of climate policy at Berlin-based think tank Climate Analytics.

Over Bolsonaro's four-year term, an estimated 45,586km2 of the Amazon was destroyed, an area bigger than the size of Denmark. And the forest is not as resilient as it once was, with scientists warning that parts of it are now emitting more carbon than they absorb.

Lula came to office with a message of protection for the Amazon. Besides calling for an end to deforestation by 2030, he increased monitoring of the forest and strengthened Brazil's environmental enforcement agency IBAMA.

Deforestation has plummeted under his leadership, with 2026 set to be its lowest level in a decade. That represents a 41% drop overall compared to Jair Bolsonaro's tenure.

Experts have already criticized Flávio Bolsonaro's record on forest protection. As a senator in 2019, he authored draft legislation that could have stark impacts for the Amazon. While landowners are currently required to preserve 80% of their property for the growth of native plants, the bill would allow them to use their holdings as they please.

"The signal from the president will say 'now you can deforest' or 'it's harder to deforest,'" said Ana Yang, director of the Environment and Society Center at London-based think tank Chatham House.

"The moment that you decrease enforcement capability, deforestation grows," she told DW.

Bolsonaro has also pledged to end illegal deforestation by 2029, a year before Lula. But Claudio Angelo is critical of that message.

"He will end illegal deforestation not by enforcing the law, but by making it legal," he said.

More generally, environmental experts fear Bolsonaro might dismantle many of the protections strengthened under the current president.

"Unfortunately, climate change has become a partisan issue, so rather than offering a solution from their perspective, the right pictures climate change as an invented problem...that regulation goes against economic growth or it goes against competitiveness, that it's the aim of the left to control the means of production," Forner said.

In an interview with Brazilian media in August, Bolsonaro said he regarded extreme weather events to be cyclical and did not believe they were solely linked to human influence.

A Bolsonaro win is likely to see Brazil move away from its position as a climate leader, a role the country embraced last year as it hosted the COP30 climate conference in the Amazonian city of Belem.

But even a Lula victory would not represent a straightforward climate success story, say experts. While the current administration has overseen significant reductions in deforestation, it has also backed plans to expand oil production.

Angelo said the decision to allow exploratory drilling was a "betrayal" of Lula's mandate but added that the president's overall record on climate had been "quite impressive".

"Lula is the world's worst climate leader, except for all the others," he told DW.

The current president will face a runoff election with Bolsonaro on October 25. But while experts say the outcome could determine the fate of the Amazon and the wider efforts to curb global warming, for many Brazilians climate is not high on their list of priorities.

"Ultimately what people care about is access to education, sanitation and health," said Yang. A road built through the Amazon to access those services, while criticized from outside Brazil for destroying parts of the rainforest, would be desirable to voters, she added.

"They don't have time to care. Not because they don't want to. They care about their own survival," she said.

Unai Emery’s side will be relieved that they took a maximum nine points from their opening three games as their fixtures in this competition are getting a lot harder. Unai Emery has managed more than 1,100 matches but will never forget the drama of “La Remontada” as he returns to the scene on Tuesday night.

Emery is back at the Nou Camp in the Champions League for the first time since one of the most epic games in the history of the competition. While in charge of Paris St-Germain nine years ago, Emery took his team to Barcelona with a 4-0 lead from the round-of-16 first leg. Yet he was left stunned as Barcelona recovered to win the rematch 6-1, with three goals in the final seven minutes and the winner proving hugely controversial.

Sergi Roberto’s goal five minutes into added time caused a massive backlash as PSG claimed it was offside, with Emery claiming on Monday that the match showed that VAR was “necessary”.
